title: Orsen and the Confession
premise: Dominic Vasquez has spent two decades as the invisible voice of Halvern Taxi's night dispatch, cataloging the town's confessions without ever becoming one. When twin letters arrive — one confessing to the unsolved 2004 fire that killed the Aldrich patriarch, the other promising a second confession 'from the one you think is dead' — Dominic realizes the letters were addressed not to him, but to the name he abandoned twenty years ago. Following the letters' clues, Dominic discovers the fire's sole witness faked her death and has been hiding in plain sight as the taxi company's aging bookkeeper, and that Dominic's own late mother helped cover up the crime to protect the man Dominic now works for. In the end, Dominic must choose between publishing the truth that will destroy the town's beloved founding family — and the last fragile memory he has of his mother — and finally steps out of the dark to testify, trading invisibility for a self that can be seen.
about_author: Wendell Yarrow is a former municipal records clerk who spent eleven years filing other people's secrets before turning to fiction. He writes at night, he says, because 'that's when towns tell the truth.'

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Night
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A slow night shift establishes Dominic's ritualized invisibility: logging fares, filing complaints, memorizing the town through radio static. A closing beat — a fare request from an address that burned down in 2004 — unsettles the routine and hints the past is calling the dispatch line.

chapters.title: Twin Envelopes
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Two letters arrive in the morning mail, both addressed to 'D. Vasquez' — but in handwriting Dominic hasn't seen in twenty years: his own childhood hand, or a perfect forgery. The first confesses to the Aldrich fire; the second promises 'the witness you buried is still breathing.' Fear and recognition war in him.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, intercut with a 2004 newspaper clipping. We learn the fire killed Edmund Aldrich, was ruled accidental, and that a witness — a teenage girl named Ruth Calloway — drowned a week later. Dominic's mother drove the coroner home that night. The emotional beat: grief he's kept alphabetized begins to spill.

chapters.title: The Boss's Kindness
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Martin Aldrich, the fire victim's son and owner of the taxi company, is warm, generous, and watchful. He mentions the mail came early. Dominic realizes Martin may have seen the letters. The beat is dread dressed as gratitude — kindness as a surveillance technique.

chapters.title: A Dead Woman's Utility Bill
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Following the second letter's clue, Dominic pulls municipal records and finds Ruth Calloway's 'death' was certified by a doctor who retired the same week — and that a utility account in her name is still active. Someone dead is paying for electricity. Hope arrives disguised as a clerical error.

chapters.title: The Bookkeeper's Hands
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic studies Marla, the company's elderly bookkeeper: her left-handed penmanship, a burn scar she calls a kitchen accident, the way she flinches at the word 'Aldrich.' He says nothing. The emotional beat is the terrible intimacy of recognizing someone who is also hiding.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, alternating Dominic and Marla. A third letter arrives, this one sent through the dispatch system itself — a fare logged from Ruth's childhood address. Marla, revealed to be Ruth in her own brief section, decides the letters are a trap set by Martin. Two hunters, each convinced the other is bait.

chapters.title: Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Searching his late mother's belongings, Dominic finds a ledger of small cash payments marked 'M.A.' spanning fifteen years — hush money, or guilt money, paid to his mother. The revelation that she was complicit lands like a second death. He drinks, then files the ledger under a false name, as he was taught.

chapters.title: The Confession That Promised More
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic deciphers the second letter's postmark: it was mailed from inside the taxi depot. The confessor isn't outside the walls — the letters are being written by someone who watches him every night. Paranoia reorganizes the entire cast; even the reader's sympathies tilt.

chapters.title: Marla's Version
chapters.summary: Marla/Ruth's POV. A full chapter in Ruth's voice: she saw Martin's father die, she saw who set the fire, and she let the town believe she drowned because the sheriff was on the Aldrich payroll. She has been writing the letters — not to trap Dominic, but because she is dying and wants the truth to outlive her.

chapters.title: Two Truths in One Depot
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs converge. Dominic corners Marla in the records room; she neither confirms nor denies, but slides him a key to a bus-station locker. The scene is a duel conducted entirely in filing terminology. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets negotiating a surrender neither trusts.

chapters.title: The Locker
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The locker holds Ruth's original statement to the sheriff, never filed, and a photograph: his mother, young, standing with the sheriff and Martin's father outside the burning house — not fleeing it. Dominic's inheritance is finally named: not money, but complicity, passed down like eye color.

chapters.title: What Martin Knows
chapters.summary: Dominic and Martin's POV split. Martin invites Dominic to dinner and, over the meal, tells his own version: his father was dying of cancer and asked for the fire — a mercy, Martin claims, arranged with Ruth's help. The confession is seductive, plausible, and almost certainly a test. Dominic lies for the first time in the book.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Successor
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic approaches the current sheriff with the statement and is met not with corruption but with exhaustion: the department's records from 2004 were 'lost in a flood' that never happened. The beat is disillusionment — the system isn't evil, just gutted, and gutted things protect whoever feeds them.

chapters.title: A Fare to the Cemetery
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, night shift. A dispatch call sends a cab to Ruth Calloway's grave; Dominic drives it himself. At the cemetery he finds fresh flowers and tire tracks — someone visits a grave they know is empty. He waits in the dark and, for the first time, chooses to be seen watching.

chapters.title: The Fourth Letter
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The final letter arrives, addressed this time to his real name — the one he abandoned. It gives a time and place: the depot, midnight, 'bring the ledger.' Dominic understands he has been managed from the start, that his investigation was the confessor's plan. The beat is terror and strange relief: invisibility ending whether he wills it or not.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Depot
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. Dominic arrives to find Marla and Martin already there, each summoned by a letter neither wrote — and a recorder running. The true confessor is the retired dispatcher who trained Dominic, the man who filed everything, including the fire, and who is dying with the archive in his head. The climax begins as testimony.

chapters.title: The Fifth Voice
chapters.summary: The old dispatcher's POV. He confesses fully: he drove the getaway, kept the ledger's twin, and chose Dominic — the son of a guilty woman — as his heir, believing inheritance demands a witness. Martin denies everything; Marla produces the statement. The emotional beat is the corruption of memory itself: three versions of one night, each sincerely held.

chapters.title: What the Tape Can't Hold
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The recorder is seized — by whom is ambiguous — and the confession exists now only in the memories of four people, two of them dying. Martin offers Dominic his mother's ledger back, destroyed, and a raise. The temptation is total: silence as inheritance, offered politely.

chapters.title: Going on Record
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic chooses visibility: he walks the recorded reconstruction of the night to the state attorney general, with Marla beside him, her death certificate in hand. Martin is charged; the town's founding story cracks open. The beat is not triumph but vertigo — the first morning in twenty years Dominic is legible to everyone.

chapters.title: The Witness Everyone Swears Is Dead
chapters.summary: Marla/Ruth's POV. Ruth testifies, old and alive and terrified, and finds that being seen does not kill her. She and Dominic share the quiet aftermath: two people unburied. Martin's trial looms unresolved, but the emotional arc completes — memory, once spoken, stops belonging to the powerful.

chapters.title: Dispatch
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, final shift. Dominic resigns, but first answers one last call and logs it plainly, in his own name. He mails the ledger — his mother's, the true one — to the attorney general, and keeps only the first letter. Closing beat: he alphabetizes nothing. He lets the file stay open, because some things should stay found.
